title: Your body almost completely paralyses itself while you dream
body: During rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, the stage of vivid dreams, the brain inhibits the motor neurons driving your muscles. The result, called **REM atonia**, is an almost complete paralysis: the eyes move in tandem and small twitches get through, but you can’t act out what you’re dreaming. Adults spend 20 to 25% of a night in REM, about 90 to 120 minutes, in cycles of roughly 90 minutes, the first episode arriving about 70 minutes after falling asleep. When the switch fails, in REM sleep behaviour disorder, people physically act out their dreams.

slides.label: of an adult’s sleep is REM: about 90 to 120 minutes a night

slides.heading: A night in cycles
items: First REM episode about 70 minutes after falling asleep
Non-REM and REM alternate in cycles of about 90 minutes
Early REM episodes last about 15 minutes, later ones about 25
Some dreaming happens in non-REM sleep too

slides.heading: Found in 1953
slides.text: Nathaniel Kleitman and his student Eugene Aserinsky defined rapid eye movement in 1953 and linked it to dreaming. During REM the brain’s supply of three chemical messengers, norepinephrine, serotonin and histamine, is shut off completely, while the body lies still.

slides.question: What goes wrong in REM sleep behaviour disorder?
slides.explanation: Without REM atonia the body is free to move, and people physically act out their dreams.
